title: Klin et al., 'Texting insincerely: the role of the period in text messaging' (Binghamton, Computers in Human Behavior 2015); via news coverage
rule: In a text, a final period on a short positive reply (Okay, Sure, Yeah, Yup) was rated less sincere than the same reply without one; handwritten notes showed no such effect. Exclamation marks rated most sincere. Klin's own caveat: punctuation is read differently in texts, not 'periods = insincere' as a law. N=126 undergraduates, one-word replies only, so do not extend to long messages.
example: 'Sure.' reads as stiff or curt; 'Sure' or 'Sure!' reads warm
llm_tell: LLM chat replies end every message and every short answer with a full stop and full sentences; in a casual register that is the marked, cold form.

title: Science Friday: Gretchen McCulloch on Because Internet (fetched excerpt)
rule: Ellipses split by age: older writers use them as a generic separator between phrases; younger writers use line/message breaks as the separator, so an ellipsis means something left unsaid, trailing off (sincere or sarcastic). Conventions clash when each side reads the other's mark by its own rules. Age is an imperfect guide; internet experience matters more. Pick the convention of the writer you are imitating and hold it.
example: Older: 'Thanks...see you at 5...' vs younger: separate short messages
llm_tell: A single uniform punctuation system (full stops, em dashes, semicolons) with no generational or personal marking.

title: McCulloch blog: texting periods (fetched; mostly points to NYT piece)
topic: typographical tone of voice, chapter contents
rule: Confirms chapter scope: periods and ellipses as tone, all-caps yelling, asterisks/tildes for emphasis, all-lowercase 'minimalist typography', leetspeak. Page itself gives no new data.

title: Because Internet (via search summaries of Wikipedia, Swarthmore Phoenix, NPR; book text not read)
topic: typographical tone: lowercase, lol, caps, repeated letters
rule: From secondary summaries of McCulloch, not the book: (1) all-lowercase is deliberate minimalist/deadpan tone, since phone autocorrect capitalises by default, so a lowercase writer is making a choice; (2) 'lol' no longer marks laughter but irony/goodwill and gives plausible deniability ('you look good in red lol'); (3) ALL CAPS reads as shouting, and caps equals yelling already in 1984 Usenet; (4) repeated letters carry prosody (rhythm, stretch). Treat each as a habit a given writer has or lacks, not a decoration to scatter.
example: you look good in red lol / nooooo / ok
llm_tell: Capitals and full punctuation everywhere; no lowercase deadpan, no softeners used as tone. When an LLM does add 'lol' or stretched letters it tends to scatter them evenly.

title: Tagliamonte & Denis 2008, 'Linguistic ruin? LOL! Instant messaging and teen language', American Speech 83(1) (via search summary; page fetch returned 403)
topic: CMC corpus: IM is conservative, mixed register
rule: Corpus of 72 Toronto teens, over a million words of natural unmonitored IM. Stereotyped 'text speak' markers (lol, abbreviations, emoticons) were only about 3 percent of the data (press-reported figure); the rest was conventional vocabulary and grammar. IM is a hybrid register mixing the full range of variants in the community, and is more formal than speech. Casual written chat is mostly ordinary words with a thin layer of markers, not wall-to-wall slang.
llm_tell: Over-slanged 'how do you do, fellow kids' imitation (every sentence carries a marker) is the wrong shape; so is zero markers.

title: Palin et al. 2019, 'How do People Type on Mobile Devices?' (MobileHCI; pdftotext of saved PDF, grep of key lines only)
rule: 37,370 volunteers: 36.2 WPM average, 2.3% uncorrected errors (Levenshtein-based, transcription task so errors are against a given sentence). 74% use two thumbs. Autocorrection associated with better performance, word prediction with worse. Takeaway for an imitator: phone text is mostly clean because autocorrect fixes slips; what survives is a few wrong-word autocorrect hits, missed spaces, and uncorrected tail errors, not scattered letter noise.
llm_tell: Humanizer text with several typos per sentence overshoots the measured ~2% rate and ignores that autocorrect, not the writer, decides which errors survive.

title: MIT undergraduate thesis on phone vs laptop typing (via search summary only)
rule: Participants typed about 20% faster on laptop keyboards than phone keyboards; misspellings were the commonest error type; misplaced spaces about 20% of phone errors. Small student thesis; low weight. Device shapes error type: phone gets space/autocorrect/wrong-word errors, desktop gets key-adjacent and transposition slips.

title: Spelling Correction with Denoising Transformer (typo statistics, via search summary; Damerau 1964 and Grudin 1983 figures second-hand)
rule: Over 80% of misspelled words contain a single error (Damerau, as cited second-hand). Category shares from one 2021 correction-pair dataset: about 39% substitution, 33% insertion, 18% deletion, 11% transposition (that dataset, not universal). Keyboard proximity and phonetics drive substitutions; a lecture deck attributes to Grudin 1983 that adjacent-key substitutions are 83% of novice substitutions vs 51% for experts (unverified). Practical rule: a real typo is one slip in one word, adjacent-key, doubled, dropped or swapped letter, not a garbled word.
llm_tell: Fake typos that are not keyboard-plausible, or that hit the same word type, or several within one sentence.

title: DAMAGE: Detecting Adversarially Modified AI Generated Text (2025)
rule: Tested 19 humanizer/paraphraser tools. Typo injection was NOT tested as a technique; the paper only lists 'introduces typos' and 'punctuation errors' as flaws in lower-tier humanizer output (stray characters, hallucinated citations, unreadable text). Detector TPR at 5% FPR on humanized text: GPTZero 60%, RADAR 5%, Binoculars 28%, a fine-tuned DAMAGE detector 98%. Synonym-swapping hurt Binoculars most (43.5%). Lesson: surface noise and synonym swaps change little at the model-detector level, and tool-made flaws are themselves visible. No direct evidence on how human readers judge injected typos. Null on that question.
llm_tell: Synonym swaps and random noise leave the underlying uniform rhythm intact.

title: Blog on bypassing AI detection / humanizers (search summary only; low reliability)
rule: Opinion only, untested: the hard part of imitating human imperfection is the natural frequency and distribution of the flaws; uniform, artificial-looking errors are the giveaway. I found no controlled study of human readers detecting injected typos. Treat 'random typos read fake' as an inference from the error-distribution data above (errors are few, single, device-shaped, person-specific), not a measured result.

title: Do LLMs produce texts with 'human-like' lexical diversity? (2025)
rule: Compared four ChatGPT versions (3.5, 4, o4-mini, 4.5) with 240 L1/L2 human writers on six lexical-diversity dimensions: ChatGPT differed significantly from humans on every one, and newer models were less human-like. Abstract gives no direction per measure, so I cannot say 'narrower' or 'wider' from this paper. Other results from search summaries conflict: some studies find LLM text lower in STTR/MTLD than human news text, one finds higher raw TTR (length-confounded). The claim 'casual human vocabulary is narrower and more repetitive than an LLM's' is NOT supported by what I read.
llm_tell: Unsettled: the measured fact is only that LLM diversity profiles do not match human ones; direction depends on the measure and length.

title: Stylometry and idiolect (search summaries of survey papers)
rule: Authorship work treats an author's idiolect as a set of character-, lexical- and structure-level habits that are stable and detectable; averaged features hide within-author spread. I found no study measuring within-author drift in capitalisation or acronym forms over a message (null). So 'capitalisation lapses as a message goes on' is an observation to apply cautiously, not a measured pattern.
llm_tell: No stable idiolect: each message is consistent with the house style, not with a person's own habits.
